passage:
Dear Meenal,

You asked how the new team is going. Honestly, a little bruised. Kamal, who joined three months ago, keeps saying in stand-ups that "some people" hand over work without context. Everyone knows who "some people" is. It stung more than I expected.

I sat with it for a weekend and asked myself what Kamal might have felt. I did skip the walkthrough on the last two tasks because I was rushed. That could feel like being left to swim alone.

So on Monday I asked Kamal for coffee and said so, plainly. Kamal went quiet, then admitted the tasks had been confusing. I still won't lower the review bar, and I said that too. I don't need to be liked by everyone. I just want to be fair. 🙂

Yours,
Arohi

qa.q: What did Kamal say in stand-ups that stung Arohi?
qa.a: Kamal said that "some people" hand over work without context, and everyone knew it meant Arohi.

qa.q: What did Arohi wonder about Kamal's feelings over the weekend?
qa.a: Arohi wondered whether Kamal felt left alone with confusing tasks, since Arohi had skipped the walkthrough twice while rushed.

qa.q: What could Arohi do if the tension returns?
qa.a: Arohi could keep giving a short walkthrough with each task and keep the review bar the same, so help and standards go together.

qa.q: How might Kamal have experienced the coffee invitation?
qa.a: Kamal may have felt nervous at first, then relieved that the confusion was heard rather than punished, even though the review standard stayed the same.

grounding: Arohi feels stung by a junior's criticism, reflects on what the junior felt, talks openly, and keeps the same standards.

Nikita heard it through the glass wall of the Indiranagar agency's meeting room: Aditi, her junior copywriter, telling two interns, "Don't bother, she'll rewrite it anyway. Total control freak."
The words stung for the rest of the afternoon. On the auto home, Nikita made herself look at it honestly. She had rewritten Aditi's last three headlines without a word of explanation. She had sent notes at eleven at night. From the outside, it must have felt like nothing Aditi did counted.
On Monday she asked Aditi for ten minutes. "I heard what you said on Friday. I think I've given you reasons to feel that. When I change your work, I'll tell you why from now on." Aditi's eyes widened, then she nodded.
"But the client deadline stays Thursday, and drafts still come to me first. That part isn't changing."

qa.q: What did Aditi call Nikita in front of the interns?
qa.a: A total control freak, saying Nikita would rewrite it anyway.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling on the auto ride home?
qa.a: She felt stung and uneasy, and as she looked honestly at her own habits she felt a pang of guilt about how Aditi had been treated.

qa.q: How did Nikita respond without dropping her standards?
qa.a: She spoke to Aditi openly, admitted her part, promised to explain her edits, and kept the Thursday deadline and review process.

qa.q: How might Aditi have experienced Nikita's rewrites before Monday?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt dismissed and frustrated, as if nothing she wrote counted, which fed the resentment she voiced to the interns.

grounding: A junior speaks against the protagonist; she feels stung, reflects on how her behaviour felt to them, speaks openly, and keeps her standards.

"Indu, got a minute before you go?"
"Service is over, chef. I'm tired."
"Two minutes." Karthik wiped his hands on his apron. "Ravi told me you said I'm a bully who likes shouting at the new cooks."
Indu folded her arms. "So?"
"So I was angry for about an hour. Then I thought about last Saturday. I shouted at you in front of the whole line over a burnt sauce. That was humiliating for you, wasn't it?"
A pause. "Yes."
"I'm sorry for that. Next time I'll tell you at the pass, quietly."
"Okay." Her arms loosened a little.
"But the sauces still get tasted before they go out. Every single one. That's not me being a bully, that's the job."
"I know," Indu muttered. "I just wanted you to say the first part."
"Fair. Go home. See you at ten."

qa.q: What did Ravi tell Karthik that Indu had said?
qa.a: That Karthik was a bully who liked shouting at the new cooks.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he first heard what Indu said, and how did it shift?
qa.a: He felt angry and stung for about an hour, then uneasy as he remembered shouting at her in front of the whole line.

qa.q: Which part of Karthik's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: He owned the public shouting, apologised, and promised quieter feedback, while keeping the tasting rule, so Indu felt respected without the standard slipping.

qa.q: Why might Indu say she just wanted to hear the first part?
qa.a: Indu seems to have needed the apology more than a change in rules; being acknowledged let her accept the standards.

grounding: A junior speaks against the protagonist; he reflects on how his behaviour felt, speaks openly with her, and holds his standards.
